appraisal_events.evidence: Françoise has condolences ready before every humiliation, and his attempts to claim success break against her « incrédulité respectueuse » and her sense of her own infallibility; Jupien then reveals that she says « que je ne valais pas la corde pour me pendre et que j'avais cherché à lui faire tout le mal possible ». The narrator at once asks whether she meant it or said it to set Jupien against him.
appraisal_events.explanation: The servant who reads him best is reported to hold him in savage contempt, and his own counter-narratives collapse before her silent knowledge; the passage deliberately leaves the sincerity of the verdict undecidable.

appraisal_events.evidence: He has chosen to love « la femme qui réunissait peut-être le plus d'avantages différents et aux yeux de qui... je ne pouvais espérer avoir aucun prestige », as rich as the richest commoner, with a personal charm « qui la mettait à la mode, en faisait entre toutes une sorte de reine », while he walks her street each morning, « solitaire, humilié », displeasing her and unable to stop.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narration installs the duchess at an unreachable height — a queen of the fashionable world — and measures the narrator's position by the distance, down to the compensatory fantasy of her ruined and begging asylum from him.

appraisal_events.evidence: « L'amitié, l'admiration que Saint-Loup avait pour moi, me semblaient imméritées et m'étaient restées indifférentes. Tout d'un coup j'y attachai du prix, j'aurais voulu qu'il les révélât à Mme de Guermantes. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Saint-Loup's esteem is stated as an established fact and suddenly becomes a currency the narrator wants spent on his behalf, even as he calls it undeserved.

status_effects.explanation: Inside his own household he is reported to be judged worthless and malicious, and the passage grants Françoise the discernment that makes such a verdict weigh.
She holds the truth about him, cannot be deceived by his boasts, and remains opaque in return: he cannot even establish whether she loves or detests him.
The passage frames her as fashion's queen, uniting rank, wealth and charm, before whom the narrator can have no prestige at all.
His need to be seen by her overrides the shame of displeasing her; he is reduced to daily humiliation in the street and to imagining her ruin as the only route to parity.
Separately from the household verdict, he is credited with the admiration of a Guermantes nephew, a hidden privilege the passage treats as real.

ambiguities: Whether Françoise's reported contempt is sincere or a maneuver aimed at Jupien is raised and left open by the passage itself, which makes the direction of the verdict on the narrator undecidable rather than merely hedged.
